analysis.one_liner: Halts large meatpacking, food, seed, and grocery-store mergers until Congress rewrites antitrust rules for food.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in the House, dying in committee at the end of the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would freeze mergers among large agribusinesses, food and beverage makers, farm-input companies, and grocery retailers until Congress passes a broader law dealing with concentration in the food system. It would also create a twelve-member commission to study the problem and recommend legal changes. The stated aim is to give family farmers and food shoppers more bargaining power against the handful of firms that dominate meatpacking, seed, and food processing.
analysis.who_benefits: Family farmers and ranchers selling cattle, hogs, grain, and milk into concentrated markets; contract poultry and hog growers; food-chain workers facing merger-driven layoffs and wage suppression; and shoppers paying grocery prices that have not fallen when farm prices do. Rural communities whose local economies decline as farms disappear would also gain if consolidation slows.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Family farmers, food workers, and grocery shoppers

how_it_helps.text: It blocks new mergers between large food and agribusiness firms — a company with more than $160 million in sales or assets could not buy a rival above $16 million — until comprehensive antitrust legislation passes, with an Attorney General waiver only for extraordinary circumstances like insolvency. [S3]

It creates a commission, with seats reserved for working farmers and organized labor, to study how concentration affects farm incomes, worker wages, rural communities, the environment, and supermarket prices, and to recommend changes to antitrust law. [S3]

The bill's findings document the stakes: the top four beef packers now control 85 percent of the market, up from 32 percent, and four infant-formula companies control nearly 90 percent of that market, a concentration level the bill links to the 2022 formula shortage. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Large agribusiness firms, meatpackers, seed and chemical companies, and grocery chains that would have to delay or abandon acquisitions while the moratorium runs. Large grocers and food manufacturers could no longer buy rivals, which could slow some consolidation-driven efficiencies; the commission costs up to $2 million in authorized appropriations.

drawbacks.text: The moratorium is open-ended: it does not end until Congress passes new comprehensive legislation, so a gridlocked Congress could leave major deals blocked indefinitely, including potentially pro-competitive ones; the waiver authority is narrow. [S3]
Blocking mergers does nothing to undo the concentration that already exists — the 85 percent beef-packers' share would remain — so the bill is a freeze, not a fix. [S3]

Critics of merger moratoria generally argue that blanket bans can prevent mergers that would lower costs or rescue failing firms; the bill's insolvency waiver addresses only part of that concern. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For farmers facing four-firm market shares of 70-90 percent in beef, pork, and grain, a freeze on further consolidation addresses a real and documented bargaining-power problem, and the $2 million commission is cheap. The main honest objection is design: a moratorium stops the bleeding without treating the underlying wound, and its open-ended duration gives Congress an easy excuse never to pass the follow-up law that would lift it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Agriculture and Judiciary Committees for its entire life; it was referred to the Agriculture Committee and the Judiciary Committee on introduction, and later to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law, where it died when the Congress ended in January 2023. [S1] [S5]

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Pocan introduced the bill on May 18, 2022, with 9 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support on the record. [S1] [S4]
The Speaker's referral sent it to two committees — Agriculture and Judiciary — a common routing that makes passage harder because a bill must win approval in each committee with jurisdiction. [S5]

In November 2022 it was referred to the House Judiciary Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law; no hearing, markup, or committee vote on the bill appears in its action history. [S5]
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died without ever reaching the House floor. [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large agribusiness, meatpacking, seed, and grocery companies that would have been covered by the merger moratorium keep full freedom to merge and acquire, because no committee ever acted on the bill and it never came to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 9 recorded cosponsors were Democrats; the bill never advanced far enough for a floor vote that would show the broader House's position. [S4]

industries.note: The bill would bar mergers among large packers during the moratorium. The top four beef packers already control 85 percent of the market, giving them leverage over the cattle prices ranchers receive. [S3]

Large agricultural input suppliers are covered by the moratorium. Three firms already control about two-thirds of the world's commodity-crop seeds, and corn seed costs have roughly quadrupled for farmers over two decades. [S3]
Large processors could not acquire rivals above the bill's size thresholds during the freeze, slowing further consolidation of the processing stage of the food chain. [S3]
Large retailers are covered by the moratorium, limiting supermarket consolidation that has widened the gap between farm prices and shelf prices. [S3]
The bill aims to stop further concentration of the buyers farmers sell to, preserving what bargaining power remains, though it does not restore markets already lost. [S3]
